title: E2: 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane and sodium hydride

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: Hydride takes a hydrogen from one of the {{CH2}} groups next to the C-Br carbon. The C-H electrons become the C=C and bromide leaves, all in the same step. Hydride and the hydrogen it took leave as {{H2}}.
steps.why: NaH is {{Na+}} and {{H-}}, a very strong base. The carbon that carries Br is tertiary, so its back side is blocked and {{SN2}} cannot happen. A strong base does not wait for bromide to leave by itself: rate = k[RBr][{{H-}}].
hints: Hydride has the electrons. Will it act as a base or try to reach a carbon with three ethyl groups on it?
A base takes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the C-Br carbon. All three {{CH2}} groups are equivalent, so pick any one.
Three arrows: hydride lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond, the C-Br bond to Br.

takeaway: Tertiary halide plus a strong base: E2, one step, three arrows, no intermediate.

title: E1: 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane in water

steps.name: Ionization (rate-determining)
steps.say: The C-Br bond breaks by itself. Bromine takes both electrons and a tertiary carbocation is left.
steps.why: Water is a weak base and a poor nucleophile, so nothing pushes bromide out. The halide can ionize because the carbocation is tertiary and water, a polar protic solvent, stabilizes both ions. Only the halide is in this slow step: rate = k[RBr].
hints: There is no strong base in the flask, so water does nothing in the first step.
Break the C-Br bond. Which atom keeps the electrons?

steps.name: Water removes a neighbouring hydrogen
steps.say: Water is the base. A lone pair on oxygen takes a hydrogen from a {{CH2}} next to the positive carbon, and the C-H electrons become the C=C.
steps.why: A hydrogen next to a carbocation is acidic enough for a weak base like water to remove. If water attacks the positive carbon instead, the product is the {{SN1}} alcohol: the two reactions share this carbocation.
hints: Water is the only base present.
The positive carbon has no hydrogen of its own. Take one from a {{CH2}} next to it.
Two arrows: O lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond.

takeaway: E1 is two steps: the leaving group leaves first, then a weak base takes a neighbouring hydrogen. The base leaves as {{H3O+}}.

title: E2: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane and methoxide (Saytzeff alkene)

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: Methoxide takes a hydrogen from the {{CH2}} next to the C-Br carbon. The C-H electrons become the C=C as bromide leaves.
steps.why: Methoxide is a strong base and the carbon is tertiary, so the reaction is {{E2}}. Methoxide is small, so it can reach the inner {{CH2}}, and taking that hydrogen gives the more substituted (Saytzeff) alkene, 2-methyl-2-butene.
hints: Strong base, tertiary carbon. Substitution or elimination?
Two kinds of neighbouring hydrogen: on the {{CH2}} and on the {{CH3}} groups. A small base gives the more substituted alkene.
Three arrows: O lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond, the C-Br bond to Br.

takeaway: A small strong base with a good leaving group gives the Saytzeff alkene by E2.

title: E1: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in methanol

steps.name: Ionization (rate-determining)
steps.say: With no strong base present, the C-Br bond breaks first. Bromide leaves with both electrons and a tertiary carbocation remains.
steps.why: Methanol is a weak base, so it cannot pull a hydrogen off the halide directly. It is a polar protic solvent, which helps the tertiary halide ionize. rate = k[RBr].
hints: Methanol alone is not a strong base. What has to happen first?
One arrow: the C-Br bond to Br.

steps.name: Methanol removes a neighbouring hydrogen
steps.say: A lone pair on the oxygen of methanol takes a hydrogen from the {{CH2}} next to the positive carbon. The C-H electrons become the C=C.
steps.why: Losing the hydrogen from the {{CH2}} gives the more substituted alkene. If methanol attacks the positive carbon instead, the {{SN1}} ether forms: same carbocation, different second step.
hints: The base is neutral methanol, not methoxide.
Two arrows: O lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond.

takeaway: Solvent alone with a tertiary halide: ionize first, then the solvent takes a hydrogen. Two steps, three arrows in all.

title: SN2 with inversion: (S)-2-butyl tosylate and hydrosulfide

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: A lone pair on sulfur attacks the carbon from the side opposite the tosylate, and the C-O bond breaks at the same time. The other three groups on the carbon flip over: inversion.
steps.why: {{HS-}} is an excellent nucleophile (126,000 in the lecture table) and a weak base, the carbon is secondary, and DMSO is polar aprotic: every condition for {{SN2}}. rate = k[ROTs][{{HS-}}].
hints: Which species has a lone pair and a negative charge?
The nucleophile attacks the carbon that carries the leaving group, from the back.
Two arrows: S lone pair to carbon, the C-O bond to oxygen.

takeaway: SN2: one step, two arrows, back-side attack. One enantiomer gives one enantiomer, inverted.

title: SN1 with racemization: 2-butyl tosylate in water

steps.name: Ionization (rate-determining)
steps.say: The C-O bond to the tosylate breaks by itself. Tosylate leaves with both electrons and a secondary carbocation remains.
steps.why: Water is a poor nucleophile, so it does not push the leaving group out. Tosylate is a good leaving group and water is a polar protic solvent that stabilizes the ions, so the bond ionizes. rate = k[ROTs].
hints: No good nucleophile is present. What happens first?
One arrow: the C-O bond to the tosylate oxygen.

steps.name: Water attacks the carbocation
steps.say: A lone pair on water attacks the positive carbon. The carbocation is flat, so water can come from the top face or the bottom face equally.
steps.why: The carbocation is {{sp2}} and planar, with an empty p orbital open on both faces. Attack on one face gives the R alcohol and attack on the other gives the S alcohol, in equal amounts: a racemic mixture.
hints: The electron-poor atom is the positive carbon.
One arrow: O lone pair to the positive carbon.

steps.name: A second water removes the extra proton
steps.say: The oxygen that just bonded has three bonds and a positive charge. Another water takes one of its hydrogens, and the O-H electrons stay on oxygen.
steps.why: A protonated alcohol is a strong acid, so the solvent removes the proton at once. This leaves the neutral alcohol and {{H3O+}}.
hints: The product so far has a positive oxygen. How does it become neutral?
Two arrows: lone pair of the new water to H, the O-H bond to oxygen.

takeaway: SN1 with water is three steps: ionize, attack, lose a proton. The flat carbocation gives both enantiomers.

title: Two E2 reactions in a row: 3,4-dibromohexane to 3-hexyne

steps.name: First E2: to the bromoalkene
steps.say: The first equivalent of base takes the hydrogen from one CHBr carbon. Its C-H electrons form the C=C and the bromide on the other carbon leaves. The product is 3-bromo-3-hexene.
steps.why: Amide ({{H2N-}}) is a very strong base and the halide is secondary: {{E2}}. The hydrogen and the bromine that leave are on neighbouring carbons.
hints: Which Br leaves: the one on the carbon losing the hydrogen, or the one on the carbon next to it?
Three arrows: N lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond, the other carbon's C-Br bond to Br.

steps.name: Second E2: to the alkyne
steps.say: The second equivalent of base takes the hydrogen on the alkene carbon next to the C-Br carbon. The C-H electrons become the second pi bond and the last bromide leaves.
steps.why: The bromoalkene still has a leaving group and a hydrogen on the next carbon, so a strong base can do {{E2}} again. Taking the hydrogen from the alkene carbon gives the alkyne. Taking one from the {{CH2}} on the other side of the C-Br carbon would give the allene instead.
hints: The remaining Br is on a C=C carbon. Which neighbouring carbon has the hydrogen that leads to a triple bond?
Three arrows again: N lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C=C (making it C≡C), the C-Br bond to Br.

takeaway: Two equivalents of strong base remove HBr twice. Each elimination is an ordinary three-arrow E2.

title: E2 with a bulky base: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane and tert-butoxide (Hofmann alkene)

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: tert-Butoxide takes a hydrogen from an end {{CH3}} group. The C-H electrons become the C=C as bromide leaves.
steps.why: tert-Butoxide is a strong base but very bulky. The hydrogens of a {{CH3}} on the outside of the molecule are easier for it to reach than the hydrogens of the inner {{CH2}}. The result is the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene, 2-methyl-1-butene.
hints: This base is large. Which hydrogens are the easiest to reach?
Take a hydrogen from a {{CH3}} attached to the C-Br carbon.
Three arrows: O lone pair to H, the C-H bond to the C-C bond, the C-Br bond to Br.

takeaway: Same halide, bulky base: the hydrogen comes from the least crowded carbon and the Hofmann alkene is major.
